components.gap: Supply the chapter's nonsymbolic/symbolic separation under its actual assumptions (numerical properties implicit vs explicitly expressed by numerals/words; nonsymbolic present in infancy, cross-species, approximate; symbolic later, human-specific, culturally variable, precise; draft pp. 2-3, 35-37) with explicit justification, and give the chapter's empirical evidence for the separation with study/task/population/uncertainty: 2-3-year-olds who count 1-10 yet fail 6>4 and give-N (Le Corre & Carey et al., p. 22); near-chance symbolic comparison of 1-9 by 3-year-olds (middle-income) and 4-5-year-olds (low-income) vs accurate K/1st graders (p. 23); numeral/dot adaptation (Piazza et al. 2007) and Diester & Nieder monkey numeral training (pp. 23-24). Lines 18-27 give only a generic dots-vs-numeral contrast without the source's assumptions or studies.

Explain the source's own noisy logarithmic mental-number-line account under its assumptions: noisy mapping from numerosity to a log-compressed continuum (Gallistel quotation, Fig. 1, pp. 10-11), Weber-Fechner ratio dependence, the claim that developmental improvement is decreasing mapping noise (pp. 11, 19) with the reported internal Weber fractions (Piazza et al. 2010: .34, .25, .15; Halberda & Feigenson 2008: .38, .11) and their populations, the small-number (<=3) exception attributed to subitizing (pp. 5, 17, 19-20), the Dehaene-Changeux numerosity-detector model (p. 12), and the log-compression account of infant/adult nonsymbolic arithmetic (log(n1)+log(n2); McCrink & Wynn 2009 6+4 / 14-4; McCrink et al. 2007 adults, pp. 17-20). The body names a compressed log code and a scalar-variability alternative (l.33-39) and proves a comparison-identification result (l.41-62, annex l.1-49), but does not state the chapter's account, its developmental-noise claim, or its supporting studies.

The log-vs-linear comparison is present for Siegler & Opfer (2003) with fits, populations and a competing proportion account, but the chapter's own comparison under its assumptions is absent: the ideal y=x (slope 1) vs Fechnerian y=k ln x framing (p. 25); the range-by-age log-to-linear sequence (0-10 preschool->K, 0-100 K->2nd, 0-1,000 2nd->4th, 0-100,000 3rd->6th; about one year later for children with mathematical learning difficulties, p. 25); and the microgenetic feedback evidence (feedback near 150 vs 725, abrupt often single-trial shift, analogy to 15 on 0-100; Opfer & Siegler 2007; Opfer & Thompson 2008; Thompson & Opfer 2008/2010, pp. 26-28) with study/task/population, and with the proportion account (l.185-317) set as its competing boundary.

Number-line estimation (2003), memory (Thompson & Siegler 2010) and arithmetic learning (Booth & Siegler 2008) are mapped with tasks, populations and measures. Missing: the chapter's measurement- and numerosity-estimation developmental results (Booth & Siegler 2006: linear fit 85%->98%, log 91%->74%; 70/30 vs 78/22 individual best fits; numerosity 43%->82%, p. 29) with task and population; Gilmore, McCarthy & Spelke (2007) approximate symbolic addition in 5-6-year-olds (60-75%, ratio-dependent, pp. 30-31); the correlational estimation-arithmetic relations (Booth & Siegler 2006; Geary et al. 2007, p. 31); and explicit conflict boundaries between the chapter's description of Booth & Siegler 2008 (training on each child's easiest incorrectly answered problems; a randomly chosen half shown bars, pp. 31-32) and the primary four-condition fixed-item design (body l.408-433), and between the chapter's nine-week and arithmetic board-game claims (pp. 34-35) and the 2008 article treated at l.592-596.

Boundaries are asserted generically (l.64-86) without the cross-species, cultural and neural claims they bound. Supply, with study/task/population/uncertainty: the species evidence (Mechner 1958 / Platt & Johnson rats; Nieder & Miller macaque single-cell log-Gaussian tuning in PFC/IPS; Diester & Nieder numeral training, pp. 10-14, 24); the infant/adult neural evidence (Izard et al. 2008 3-month-old ERP with coarse source reconstruction; Cantlon et al. 2006 and Piazza et al. 2004 fMRI, pp. 14-15, 20); the cultural claims (Butterworth et al. 2008, Gordon 2004, Pica et al. 2004, Dehaene et al. 2008 Amazonian groups, pp. 2, 36); and the chapter's competing accounts: continuous-cue account (Clearfield & Mix 1999, 2001) vs Brannon et al. 2004 and cross-modal rebuttal (pp. 7-9), object-file/subitizing vs numerical account of infant arithmetic (Simon 1997; Uller et al. 1999; McCrink & Wynn 2004, pp. 16-17), and operational momentum vs log compression (McCrink & Wynn 2009, p. 18).
